newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Precious metals dented by supply worries.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Precious metals dented by supply worries.

text.p: Precious metal prices took a battering on Tuesday as news that strikes at a Russian mine would not go ahead coincided with options-related selling.
Worst affected of the precious metals was palladium which tumbled $6.50 to $141.50 an ounce, its lowest since February 25, before recovering a little to close at $143.50.
The fall came after the Norilsk plant in Russia, the world's biggest palladium producer, announced output would not be disrupted through to June 30 as many market players had expected.

Platinum also took some punishment and skidded down $4.50 to close at $143.50. Dealers reported fund selling in all the precious metals, with the expiry of off-market March options contributing to the drop.
"This scenario happens with amazing regularity after nearly every expiry. The palladium news out of Russia doesn't help much either," a dealer said.

But traders in nickel, Norilsk's main product, were unphased by the news from Russia. The price dipped on news of a sizeable rise in London Metal Exchange warehouse stocks but then strangely whip-sawed back up on the news from Russia.
"Maybe they had been expecting the news so they turned around on the fact," one LME trader said.
Buying interest from investment funds also helped nickel to reclaim its lost ground in the afternoon to end the session at $7,780, just below Monday's close of $7,820.
Gold also tested downside resistance with bullion slipping below the key $350 level to $349.60, down from $350.90 after an uneventful off-market options expiry.

But trading in gold was largely confined to a small range as market eyes focused on a meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee, which was widely expected to hike interest rates by 25 basis points -- the first raise for over two years.
Silver slid to $5.10/$5.12, testing technical support levels.
The twice-weekly LME stock list failed to effect most base metals. Aluminium was the only real mover, falling $5 to $1,653 despite a 8,775 tonne decrease in stock.

Copper managed to make some headway with a late afternoon burst of buying on the back of a 4,300-tonne inventory fall. But prices fell back as traders shied away from the $2,380 level, with copper ending the day at $2,377.
The soft commodities had a quiet day with coffee at first continuing Monday's sell-off. But benchark May robusta futures bottomed out at $1,515 before closing at $1,568.
"There was no fund selling in New York and this helped restore some confidence in London," one trader said.
Meanwhile, Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures took heed of concerns of a deterioration in hard red winter wheat crop conditions in Texas and Oklahoma, traders said.

Floor sources also pointed to the National Weather Service six- to 10-day outlook which called for above-normal temperatures and normal to below normal precipitation across much of the HRW wheat growing season.
